newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FEATURE - Collectors, dealers vie for best Portuguese art.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Collectors, dealers vie for best Portuguese art.

text.p: Portugal's art market is going from strength to strength with private collectors seeking a good investment bidding against dealers for the best quality paintings and antiques that come up for sale.
Last month an anonymous buyer paid a record price of 42 million escudos ($244,000) for a Portuguese painting, a 1910 oil canvas by renowned local artist Jose Malhoa depicting a drunk.
The work, "Enough, My Father!", rich in colour, shows a young woman pleading to her drunken father in a bar to stop drinking.

Malhoa (1855-1933), who painted scenes of villagers and farmhands, was a leading Portuguese impressionist and was hailed in his time as one of Portugal's greatest artists. Many of his works are displayed in national museums and galleries today.

Clara Ferreira Marques, a partner at auctioneers Leiria & Nascimento, said the record price was paid because one of Malhoa's best works had come on the market, rather than because an art boom was starting in Portugal.
"Just as the best Van Gogh paintings sell for very high prices and his less impressive works sell for much less, the same is true of Malhoa's paintings," she said.
But she added: "A recovery is under way in the Portuguese fine art market."
IMPROVING ECONOMY ENCOURAGES BUYERS

Private collectors bid against dealers at auction for a wide selection of high-quality paintings, porcelain tableware, sculptures and antique clocks. Many items have been sold for well above their reserve prices.
Auctioneers say Portugal's improving economy and a climate of falling interest rates have encouraged buyers to seek better returns from paintings than cash.
"It's better to have a good painting than money in the bank," said Francisco Cabral Moncada, a well-known local dealer.
Local banks and insurance companies were active buyers of high-quality Portuguese art sold at auction, auctioneers say.
At one auction in Lisbon last month, two of Portugal's best known modern artists fetched record prices for their work.

An oil on wood showing a view across Lisbon's rooftops of the river Tagus dotted with sailboats, painted by Carlos Botelho (1899-1982) in 1944, sold for 16 million escudos ($93,000), more than three times its reserve price.
An anonymous private collector outbid a Lisbon art gallery for the work.
A brightly painted oil on canvas by Francisco Smith (1881-1961), depicting a high society picnic in a garden, fetched 6.5 million escudos ($38,000), almost double its reserve.
Auctioneers were divided over why Portuguese paintings sold for lower prices than art from other European countries.
"It's regionalism. Portugal is on the edge of the mainstream art market and its best painters are not well known. But we do have top quality works," said Cabral Moncada.
But Joao Pinto Ribeiro, president of Palacio do Correio-Velho, Portugal's biggest auction house, said foreign artists produced higher quality work than the Portuguese.

Portuguese art presented excellent investment opportunities, he said, citing the case of an English collector who recently sold at auction a Botelho depicting a view of Lisbon for 15 million escudos ($87,000).
He said the collector had paid a tiny sum for the piece some 20 years ago after spotting Botelho's talent.
NATURALISTS, IMPRESSIONISTS FETCH HIGHEST PRICES

The Portuguese artists who sell for the highest prices are naturalists and impressionists such as Malhoa, and modernists such as Botelho and Maria Helena Vieira da Silva (1908-92), perhaps Portugal's most celebrated painter, auctioneers said.
Pinto Ribeiro said that prices of paintings by Vieira da Silva, who has a museum dedicated to her abstract work in Lisbon, had dipped recently and was at a loss to explain why.
Ferreira Marques said one reason may be that few of her best quality works had come to the market lately and those who already owned her paintings were reluctant to sell them.
Views of Lisbon, a speciality of Botelho, were especially popular among Portuguese collectors, auctioneers said.
Portuguese collectors turned out in force at auctions held abroad, bidding by telephone for Portuguese paintings and furniture sold by Sotheby's and Christies.

"It was always important for Portuguese collectors to own the best paintings by Portuguese artists," said Pinto Ribeiro, whose office in an old quarter of central Lisbon is a mayhem with valuable paintings and furniture awaiting sale.
Portuguese art often sells for higher prices in foreign auctions because the sales are well publicised and attract the richest buyers, auctioneers said.
Advances in telecommunications and publicity made it easy for those who were not experts in Portuguese art to consult reference texts and bid for the best work. ($1=172.0)
